extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates / graduate students in algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, computational criteria, and structural theorems for Zariski tangent/cotangent spaces, regular local rings, and smoothness of schemes over a field; plus related results about fiber dimension and spreading-out/generic-to-open arguments. Targets learners checking singularity/regularity/smoothness and computing tangent spaces via Jacobians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski cotangent and tangent space definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Zariski cotangent space of a local ring (A,m) is m/m^2; it is a vector space over the residue field A/m. The dual vector space is the Zariski tangent space. For a scheme X, the Zariski cotangent space T^∨_{X,p} is the cotangent space of the local ring O_{X,p}, and similarly for the tangent space T_{X,p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of m/m^2 are called cotangent vectors or differentials; tangent vectors are elements of the dual. The cotangent definition is more algebraically natural and is the one to compute first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent space as derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: In analogy with differential geometry, the tangent space at p may be identified with derivations at p, which induce linear maps m/m^2 → residue_field; hence tangent vectors correspond to k-linear maps (m/m^2) → k satisfying Leibniz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to interpret tangent vectors concretely (derivations taking functions to 'derivative values' at p). Exercise 13.1.A checks the equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian computes Zariski cotangent space (Jacobian corank)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is finite type over k and locally Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr), then the Zariski cotangent space at a k-valued point p is given by the cokernel of the Jacobian map k^r → k^n given by the Jacobian matrix J = (∂fi/∂xj)(p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus dim_k T_{X,p} equals the corank of the Jacobian matrix at p. Compute by taking formal partial derivatives and evaluating at p (Exercise 13.1.I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull's principal-ideal theorem for tangent spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a ring and m a maximal ideal, then the Zariski tangent space of A/(f) at m is cut out in the Zariski tangent space of A at m by the single linear equation f (mod m^2). Hence the tangent-space dimension of Spec A/(f) at [m] is either equal to or one less than that of Spec A at [m].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: passing to a hypersurface imposes at most one linear condition on tangent vectors; use linear terms f mod m^2 to see this (Exercise 13.1.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of tangent spaces under closed subschemes/unions/intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y and Z are closed subschemes of X containing p, then T_{Z,p} is a natural sub-κ(p)-vector space of T_{X,p}; T_{Y∪Z,p} contains the span of T_{Y,p} and T_{Z,p}, and T_{Y∩Z,p} is the intersection of the respective subspaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these containments to reason about how tangent spaces change under scheme-theoretic union and intersection (Exercise 13.1.C). Note scheme-theoretic union/intersection matters; equalities can fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent map for morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π: X → Y and p ∈ X with q = π(p), the morphism of local rings O_{Y,q} → O_{X,p} induces n/n^2 → m/m^2 (and duals), giving a natural linear map T_{X,p} → T_{Y,q}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the algebraic analogue of the differential (pushforward) map on tangent spaces; it requires analyzing induced maps on maximal ideals and their squares (13.1.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitesimal description of tangent vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural bijection M or(Spec k[ε]/(ε^2), X) ↔ {a point p with residue field k and a tangent vector at p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use maps from the dual numbers Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) to X to model first-order (infinitesimal) tangent data (Exercise 13.1.G). Useful in deformation theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian corank is intrinsic and upper semicontinuous
rubrics_metrics.description: The corank of the Jacobian matrix at p (the Jacobian corank function JC: X → Z_{≥0} with JC(p) = dim_k T_{X,p}) is intrinsic to X and does not depend on presentation; JC is an upper-semicontinuous function on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence of presentation: appending relations or adding generators preserves corank (Exercise 13.1.J). Upper semicontinuity: loci where JC ≥ n are closed (Exercise 13.1.K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Noether normalization / spreading-out principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property holds over the generic fiber (after base change to the function field K(B)), then by clearing finitely many denominators (inverting a product b ∈ B) one can obtain the property over a distinguished open subset D(b) of Spec B — i.e., 'spread out' generic results to an open neighborhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in arguments that deduce a finite/good property over the generic point and then invert finitely many elements to get it generically on the base (see discussion after (12.4.2.2) and surrounding proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper semicontinuity of fiber dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X → Y a morphism of finite type k-schemes: (a) the function p ↦ (dimension of largest component of fiber of π containing p) is upper semicontinuous on X; (b) if π is closed (e.g., proper), the fiber-dimension function on Y is upper semicontinuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on dim Y and by removing the dense open where fibers have expected relative dimension (Theorem 12.4.3). Use Exercise 12.4.A and Theorem 12.2.9 as inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generically finite implies finite over a dense open
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a generically finite morphism of irreducible k-varieties of dimension n, then there exists a dense open subset V ⊂ Y above which π is finite (Proposition 12.4.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: cover X by finitely many affine opens Ui and apply finiteness over dense opens Vi for each Ui (Exercise 10.3.G), then intersect to get a common dense open V. Use closedness of π in the argument (Exercises 12.4.G–H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of regular local ring / regular point
rubrics_metrics.description: A local ring (A,m) is regular if equality holds in Theorem 12.3.12, i.e., dim_k (m/m^2) = dim A. A locally Noetherian scheme X is regular at p if O_{X,p} is a regular local ring; otherwise p is singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular = 'correct' tangent-space dimension. Dimension-0 Noetherian local ring is regular iff it is a field (Exercise 13.2.A). Regular points are geometrically well-behaved (only one irreducible component passes through a regular point, Exercise 13.2.K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian criterion for regularity (finite type over field)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X = Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) has pure dimension d, then a k-valued point p ∈ X is regular iff the Jacobian corank at p is d (Exercise 13.2.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a hands-on method to check singularity at closed points using the Jacobian; combine with the intrinsic corank/Jacobian computation (Exercise 13.1.I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular locus for a hypersurface via gradient vanishing
rubrics_metrics.description: For f ∈ k[x1,...,xn], the singular closed points of the hypersurface f = 0 in A^n_k are given by the simultaneous equations f = ∂f/∂x1 = ... = ∂f/∂xn = 0 (Exercise 13.2.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the concrete gradient-vanishing test for singularities on hypersurfaces (classical criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of smoothness over a field (k-smooth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-scheme is k-smooth of dimension d if it is pure dimension d and admits an affine open cover Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) where the Jacobian matrix has corank d at all points (not just closed points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smoothness is a relative notion that generalizes regularity; it guarantees nice local structure (and is preserved under many operations). For finite-type schemes, smoothness can be checked on any affine cover using Jacobian corank (13.2.4 and remark referencing 13.1.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness and base change independence
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is locally finite type over k and k ⊂ ℓ is a field extension, then X is smooth over k iff X ×_Spec k Spec ℓ is smooth over ℓ (Exercise 13.2.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smoothness is stable under extension of the base field; check after base change to simplify verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth ⇒ regular; regular ⇒ smooth over perfect fields (comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every smooth k-scheme is regular (no hypothesis on perfection). If k is perfect, every regular finite-type k-scheme is smooth over k (Smoothness-Regularity Comparison Theorem 13.2.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: regularity does not in general imply smoothness when k is not perfect (counterexamples provided, e.g., k = F_p(u), X = Spec k[x]/(x^p − u)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are integral domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is a regular local ring of dimension n, then A is an integral domain (Theorem 13.2.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: at a regular point only one irreducible component passes through the point (Exercise 13.2.K); nonempty regular Noetherian schemes are irreducible iff connected (Exercise 13.2.L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Slicing criterion for regularity (effective Cartier divisor)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is Noetherian, D an effective Cartier divisor on X, and p ∈ D, then if p is a regular point of D, p is a regular point of X (Exercise 13.2.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses Krull's principal-ideal theorem for tangent spaces; slicing by Cartier divisors preserves regularity upwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular subschemes inside regular schemes give regular embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is a regular local ring of dimension n and I ⊂ A cuts out a regular local ring of dimension d (so r = n−d), then Spec A/I is a regular embedding in Spec A; more generally a closed embedding of regular schemes is a regular embedding (Exercise 13.2.M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric consequence: for smooth ambient W, codimension bounds on intersections follow (Exercise 13.2.N). Use existence of r elements whose images form a basis of I/(I∩m^2) to exhibit the embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian corank independence of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given A generated by x1,...,xn with relations I generated by f1,...,fr, appending additional relations or adding auxiliary variables and relations does not change the corank of the Jacobian matrix at a point p; hence the corank is intrinsic to A (Exercise 13.1.J).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies computing corank with any convenient presentation; shows the Jacobian corank function is well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective Jacobian corank formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective k-scheme X ⊂ P^n_k cut out by homogeneous polynomials f_i, the Jacobian corank function JC(p) equals one less than the corank of the projective Jacobian matrix (matrix of partials with respect to x0,...,xn) at p (Exercise 13.1.N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care is required because projective Jacobian entries are not global functions; interpret corank via homogeneous coordinates and the appropriate linear algebra at the point.
